Volume 13 · Chapter 07

Dynamic and repeated games

Graduate Author-reviewed · Prerequisites: v13-c06

By the endAnalyze sequential incentives and intertemporal cooperation with credible strategies.

Volume 13 · Chapter 7

From credible actions to intertemporal incentives

A threat can deter entry in a normal-form equilibrium even when carrying it out would hurt its author. A punishment can sustain cooperation only if it remains optimal when the punishment actually arrives. Private information adds another requirement: beliefs after an unexpected move must respect what players could have known. Dynamic analysis supplies complete contingent strategies, continuation incentives and a coherent information model.

Capability. Derive subgame and sequential equilibria, prove finite sequential existence, verify infinite-horizon incentives at every history, and distinguish a constructive cooperation theorem from a universal prediction. Six original worked games and twelve solved exercises connect credibility, public randomization and reputation. Payoffs are stated utility units; interpreting them as money additionally requires the corresponding risk-neutral preferences.

Prerequisites. Uncertainty and information supplies finite expected utility and Bayes’ rule; equilibrium existence proves the needed finite-dimensional fixed-point theorem. Welfare and collective choice distinguishes desirable allocations from implementable incentives. Static games and refinements proves finite Nash and strategic-form perfect-equilibrium existence, including its fully mixed best-response characterization. Here we apply that result to a precisely defined agent game and prove the additional information-set argument.

1. A plan, a move and remembered information

A finite extensive game has a finite rooted tree, a moving player or chance at every nonterminal node, finite nonempty action sets, specified chance probabilities, and a terminal utility vector. Nodes where a player cannot distinguish its position belong to one information set, with the same available actions throughout that set. Structural zero-probability chance branches and their descendants are pruned; empty information sets are removed. All remaining chance edges have positive probability. The finite existence theorem below concerns this pruned game, not rationality at events excluded by its own primitive probability law.

A pure strategy si assigns an action to every information set of player i, including sets that the strategy itself prevents reaching. A mixed strategy mi is a distribution over such complete plans. A behavioral strategy bi assigns an action distribution at each information set, with fresh independent randomization when it is reached. Opponents’ strategies are fixed when testing a unilateral deviation; changing one’s own contingent plan does not rewrite their responses.

Perfect recall means that all nodes in one information set have the same ordered sequence of that player’s previous information sets and own actions. The player remembers both what it knew and what it did. An information set then cannot be encountered twice along a path: the remembered sequence would have different lengths. Own information sets are partially ordered by possible succession, with no cycles. Perfect information, in which every player information set is a singleton, is stronger.

Finite realization equivalence. In a game with perfect recall, every mixed strategy has a behavioral strategy giving the same distribution over terminal nodes against every profile of opponents, and conversely. For the behavioral-to-mixed direction, independently select an action for every own information set before play, assigning plan si probability ∏h∈Hᵢbi(si(h)|h). Along a terminal path each own information set appears at most once. Summing over the unused plan coordinates leaves exactly the product of the action probabilities on that path. Multiplication by chance and opponents’ path probabilities gives the same terminal law.

For the converse, let Ri(h) be the set of own plans agreeing with the remembered own information/action sequence before h. Perfect recall makes this the same set for every node in h. When mi(Ri(h))>0, define

bi(a|h)=mi({s∈Ri(h):s(h)=a}) / mi(Ri(h)).

If the denominator is zero, choose any distribution at h. To prove equivalence, fix a terminal path and list its own decisions in order. The sets of plans compatible with successive own prefixes are nested; each behavioral factor is the mixed probability of the next prefix divided by that of the current one. Their product telescopes to the probability of the entire own action sequence. If a prefix first acquires zero probability, the behavioral probability of its entering action is zero too, so later arbitrary choices cannot change the terminal probability. Chance and opponents’ factors are unchanged. This holds for every terminal path and every opponent profile. It is realization equivalence, not equality of the probability distributions over unused contingent plans.

The hypotheses matter. If a player forgets a past action, a later information set may mix different own prefixes. If the same information set is visited twice, a fresh behavioral draw at each visit need not be representable by choosing one fixed action for that set in advance. Exercise 11 calculates such an absentminded counterexample. Manea’s notes, dated 19 January 2017, pages 23–28 provide the extensive-form and remembered-history setting; the telescoping and zero-prefix arguments above supply the full finite proof used here.

2. Credibility at every subgame

A subgame begins at a single known node and includes all its descendants without cutting an information set: any information set it meets is entirely included. A chance node can start a subgame. A subgame-perfect equilibrium (SPE) is a strategy profile whose restriction to every such subgame is a Nash equilibrium. The whole game counts. If there are no proper subgames, subgame perfection alone adds no restriction to Nash.

Finite backward induction. Every finite perfect-information game has a pure-strategy SPE. At the deepest player nodes choose an action maximizing the mover’s utility; at chance nodes take the specified expectation. Replace each solved continuation by its payoff vector and work toward the root, selecting any maximizing action at a tie. A finite tree makes this procedure terminate. For a proof of optimality against an arbitrary contingent deviation, induct on the remaining depth. At a player’s root node, any continuation deviation after a chosen branch cannot improve on that branch’s already optimal continuation; choosing among branches therefore cannot beat the maximizing action. At other players’ or chance nodes the same inequalities average with fixed nonnegative probabilities. Thus no unilateral deviation improves in any solved subtree. This proves SPE, not merely root optimality.

For finite games with simultaneous actions at public stages, solve the final stage by a stage-game Nash equilibrium from C06 and apply the same continuation argument. A selection among multiple continuation equilibria can affect earlier incentives; backward induction is not generally a uniqueness theorem. Distinguish a complete strategy, its induced outcome and the distribution of off-path responses.

Worked case 1: entry and a threat that cannot survive entry

An entrant first chooses Out or In. Out pays (2,3), listing entrant then incumbent. After In the incumbent chooses Fight, paying (−1,−2), or Accommodate, paying (4,1). Accommodation strictly beats fighting at the reached decision, so backward induction gives the unique SPE (In,Accommodate), with payoff (4,1).

To find all normal-form Nash equilibria, let x be the entrant’s entry probability and f the incumbent’s fight probability in its complete contingent plan. Entry gives 4−5f versus 2 from Out. Accommodation beats fighting ex ante by 3x. If x>0, the incumbent must use f=0, which makes entry strictly better and forces x=1. If x=0, every incumbent plan is a best reply, while Out is optimal exactly when f≥2/5. Hence the full Nash set is (x,f)=(1,0), together with (0,f) for f∈[2/5,1]. There is no additional partially entering equilibrium: any positive x removes the incumbent’s indifference.

Now subtract an entry cost k≥0 from both entrant payoffs following In, leaving Out and incumbent payoffs unchanged. The incumbent still accommodates at every entry node. The entrant compares 4−k with 2: it enters for k<2, stays out for k>2 and can use any mixture at k=2. The equality concerns the entrant’s action, not a license for the incumbent to fight. A sunk cost changes entry incentives without making an unprofitable continuation threat credible.

3. Beliefs are part of a sequential assessment

An assessment (b,μ) consists of a behavioral profile and, for every information set h, a probability distribution μh over its nodes. Conditional utility starts at a node drawn from μh and follows the stated continuation. Sequential rationality requires that, at every h of player i, its entire prescribed continuation be at least as good as every alternative own continuation, holding opponents fixed. A current-action comparison alone is initially a weaker requirement; Section 4 proves when it is sufficient.

A completely mixed behavior profile assigns positive probability to every available action. On the pruned finite tree it reaches every information set, so Bayes’ rule determines μh(x)=Pr(x)/Pr(h). The assessment is consistent if one common sequence of completely mixed profiles bⁿ→b has its Bayes beliefs μⁿ→μ at every information set. The same sequence must explain all beliefs. These perturbed profiles need not themselves be equilibria. A sequential equilibrium is a consistent, sequentially rational assessment. At a positive-reach information set, continuity of the Bayes ratio makes consistency agree with ordinary Bayesian updating; its extra force is at zero-reach sets.

For comparison only, call an assessment a weak PBE here if it is sequentially rational and satisfies Bayes’ rule at information sets reached with positive probability under its own profile. This explicit definition puts no other restriction on zero-reach beliefs. “Perfect Bayesian equilibrium” has several conventions; do not transfer claims about a different definition to this one.

Worked case 2: a continuation tremble cannot change nature’s odds

Player 1 chooses Stop, paying (1,1), or Continue. After Continue, nature selects H with probability 1/3 and L with probability 2/3. Player 2 observes that Continue occurred but not the state, and chooses A or B at one information set. Player 1 receives 0 under A and 3 under B in either state. Player 2 receives 3 in H and 0 in L from A, or 0 in H and 2 in L from B.

If player 2 assigns H probability θ, its values are 3θ and 2(1−θ), so A is optimal exactly when θ≥2/5. Thus Stop,A with any such θ is a weak PBE: player 1 prefers 1 to 0, and the unreached information set has no Bayes restriction under that definition.

But if a completely mixed player 1 continues with probability c>0, the node weights at player 2 are c/3 and 2c/3. Bayes’ rule gives H probability 1/3 for every c. Hence every consistent limiting assessment has θ=1/3. The actual continuation values for player 2 are (1,4/3), so it chooses B strictly, and player 1 continues strictly because 3>1. This is the unique sequential assessment. For an explicit consistency sequence, use Continue and B each with probability 1−ε, their alternatives with ε, and let ε↓0. The belief stays exactly 1/3.

In this particular tree, the chance node after Continue also starts a proper subgame containing both nodes of player 2’s information set. Solving that subgame forces B, so SPE also eliminates Stop,A. This is a counterexample to claiming that every assessment satisfying our weak-PBE definition must be subgame perfect. It is not a universal ranking of all notions called PBE.

Yildiz’s Spring 2022 notes, printed pages 104–115 distinguish assessments, common-sequence consistency and the agent-normal representation. The preceding tree and all its payoffs are original.

4. Proving finite sequential existence without skipping the information step

Own-factor cancellation lemma. Let (b,μ) be a consistent assessment in a finite perfect-recall game. Fix a starting information set h of player i, initial distribution μh, and any changed behavioral continuation βi. If a later information set k of i is reached with positive probability from this start under (βi,b−i), the conditional distribution over its nodes is μk.

Here is the proof, including the zero-reach issue. If one node of k follows h, perfect recall makes every node of k follow a node of h, through the same ordered own action sequence between h and k. Otherwise two nodes of k would disagree about whether h was visited or what i did. Let (bⁿ,μⁿ) be the completely mixed sequence certifying consistency. For every node x of k, its unconditional probability under bⁿ factors as Qⁿi(k)Rⁿ−i,0(x), where the first factor is the product of own action probabilities before k and is the same for every x∈k. The second contains opponents’ and chance factors. The positive common own factor cancels from the Bayes ratio.

More specifically, start at h with μⁿh, replace i’s continuation by βi, and leave others at bⁿ−i. Its path weight to x∈k is the original bⁿ path weight, divided by Prbⁿ(h), and multiplied by the common ratio of βi to bⁿi action products between h and k. Positive limiting reach under β implies every required β action in that remembered sequence is positive. All these multipliers therefore cancel on conditioning on k, giving exactly μⁿk. Finite path probabilities are continuous in the starting distribution and continuation strategies. Since the limiting denominator Pr(k|h,μh,βi,b−i) is strictly positive, taking the limit proves the asserted conditional belief. We did not divide by a zero limiting equilibrium reach probability. A k with zero reach under the changed continuation contributes zero to its expected payoff and needs no such conditional ratio.

Information-set one-shot lemma. For a consistent assessment in this finite perfect-recall game, sequential rationality is equivalent to having no profitable deviation that changes only the action distribution at one information set and then follows b. Necessity is immediate. For sufficiency, fix h and any changed continuation βi. Among own information sets where it differs from b, choose one maximal under possible succession. Beyond that set k its own continuation already equals b. If k is reached with positive probability from h under the changed plan, the cancellation lemma says that its actual conditional belief is μk; the assumed local inequality therefore allows replacing βi(·|k) by bi(·|k) without lowering payoff from h. If k has zero reach, the replacement has zero effect. Reach of k depends on past moves, not its own current choice. The finite acyclic own-information order permits repeating these replacements until no deviation remains. Consequently b is at least as good as β from h. Mixed current deviations add nothing because conditional payoff is linear in their action probabilities. This proves global continuation optimality, rather than assuming it.

Existence theorem. Every finite perfect-recall game with the declared positive-chance convention has a sequential equilibrium. Construct its agent-normal game: each player-information-set pair h is a separate finite strategic agent whose actions are A(h) and whose terminal expected payoff is that of the original player i(h). Independently mixing these agents is precisely a behavioral profile on the tree. C06 proves that every such finite game has a perfect profile b and a completely mixed sequence tⁿ→b such that each bh is an unconstrained best response to tⁿ−h. The other agents here include the same original player’s other information sets; this is essential.

Every h has positive reach under tⁿ. Its reach is independent of the current h-agent’s action because perfect recall prevents revisiting h. The ex ante payoff difference from changing that agent alone equals this positive reach probability times its conditional continuation payoff difference given the Bayes belief μⁿh. Divide the best-response inequality by that positive probability. The finite product of belief simplices is compact, so choose one subsequence along which every μⁿh converges to μh. Conditional continuation utilities are finite sums, continuous in beliefs and subsequent behavioral probabilities. Taking limits yields every local one-shot inequality at (b,μ), even at information sets with zero limiting reach. The sequence also certifies consistency. The information-set lemma now yields full sequential rationality and completes existence.

This proof does not replace agent-form perfection by ordinary strategic-form perfection of the original players’ complete plans; the latter can correlate their mistakes at different information sets. Nor does agent-form Nash alone suffice: without trembles, an unreached agent can be indifferent ex ante while prescribing a conditionally bad action. Sequential equilibrium implies SPE: at the known root of any subgame, the same last-deviation argument starts from a point mass. Because the subgame cuts no information set, Bayes’ rule along the completely mixed sequence cancels the common path to that root; at each subsequently reached own information set the same conditional-belief and replacement argument applies. Thus no entire subgame deviation improves payoff.

Manea’s agent-form theorem on pages 46–47 invokes a one-shot adaptation. The cancellation and finite elimination proof above supplies that missing step explicitly. No infinite-tree sequential-existence theorem, generic converse or invariance under arbitrary tree changes is asserted.

5. Repetition changes incentives, not the obligation to verify them

Let G be a finite stage game with payoffs bounded in absolute value by M. At dates t=0,1,… players observe all past action profiles, then simultaneously choose current actions. A strategy is a behavioral action rule after every finite public history. The discount factor satisfies 0<δ<1. We use the normalized value Ui=(1−δ)EΣt≥0δᵗui(aᵗ), in stage-payoff units. The unnormalized value Vi=Ui/(1−δ) is useful for continuation arithmetic. At any history, normalization gives the recursion U=(1−δ)u+δU′. A proposed strategy must specify play after deviations by either or both players.

Discounted one-shot deviation principle. A profile in this finite-action, perfect-monitoring repeated game is SPE if and only if no player gains by changing only its current action at any public history and then returning to the profile. The same statement allows a finite public signal before current actions, provided every realized-signal history is tested. Necessity follows from SPE. For sufficiency, suppose a deviation improves normalized continuation value by ε>0 at some history. Truncate it after K future stages, returning to the prescribed rule thereafter. Since the two continuations then differ only in the tail, their value difference is at most

(1−δ)Σt=K∞2Mδᵗ = 2Mδᴷ.

Choose K making this less than ε/2; the truncated deviation is still profitable. There are finitely many histories through K, including the finite public signals. At its last deviating stage, replace the deviating action after each such history by the prescribed action. Future behavior is already prescribed, so each replacement weakly improves value by the assumed one-shot inequality. Work backward to the initial history; the prescribed strategy would then dominate a strictly better deviation, a contradiction. This establishes the full infinite-horizon result. Bounded payoffs, discounting and observed histories supplied the tail and replacement arguments; the result cannot simply be asserted under arbitrary average-payoff or private-monitoring specifications.

Worked case 3: a finite end date and an infinite credible threat

Row / columnCD
C(4,4)(−1,6)
D(6,−1)(1,1)

Defection D gains 2 against either opponent action, so it is strictly dominant and DD is the unique stage Nash equilibrium. In any finite, commonly known number T of repetitions, with positive discounting and additive stage utility, the final stage prescribes DD after every history. Its continuation payoff is then independent of earlier play. The previous stage again has the same unique Nash equilibrium, and induction gives DD at every date and every history. More generally this induction applies to a fixed finite repetition of a stage game with a unique Nash equilibrium: uniqueness fixes the continuation payoff at every public history. A random or unknown end date, a changed terminal payoff or multiple continuation equilibria changes the argument’s premises.

For infinite repetition, the grim strategy begins with CC and continues CC only if every previous action pair was CC. After any other pair it plays DD forever, including after further departures. At a cooperative history, the unnormalized obedience value is 4/(1−δ); one-shot defection yields 6+δ/(1−δ). Cooperation is optimal exactly when δ≥2/5. During punishment, D beats C by 2 now and the absorbing continuation is unchanged, so punishment is credible. The one-shot principle proves SPE at and above the cutoff; below it the proposed strategy fails at its first cooperative history. For different player discounts, each player must satisfy its own δi≥2/5. This verifies a strategy; it does not claim uniqueness of infinite-horizon equilibrium or predict how people learn it.

6. Forgiveness is a continuation rule, not an exemption from incentives

Worked case 4: finite punishment with a reset rule

Use the same stage game. There is a cooperative state C, prescribing CC, and punishment states Pk, k=1,…,T, prescribing DD for k remaining periods. In C, compliance leaves C and any other action pair starts PT next period. In Pk, compliance moves to Pk−1, with P₀=C; any other pair resets to PT next period. This defines all histories, including unilateral or simultaneous departures during punishment. T is a positive integer.

Let VC=4/(1−δ) and use Pk also for the unnormalized compliant value of that state. Summing its k low-payoff periods gives

Pk=(1−δᵏ)/(1−δ)+δᵏVC,   P₀=VC.

At C, defection earns 6+δPT instead of 4+δVC. Rearrangement yields the exact cooperation constraint

2 ≤ δ(VC−PT) = 3Σt=1Tδᵗ.

At Pk, obeying gives 1+δPk−1; switching to C against D gives −1+δPT. Since δ<1, Pk−1≥PT: fewer punishment periods bring the high payoff sooner. Obedience therefore gains 2+δ(Pk−1−PT)≥2. Every punishment state is credible. The cooperation inequality is consequently necessary and sufficient for this entire automaton to be SPE.

The right side is continuous and strictly increasing in δ∈[0,1], starting at 0 and ending at 3T. Thus it crosses 2 exactly once. For T=1 the threshold is 2/3; for T=2 it is (√33−3)/6. Adding a punishment period strictly lowers the threshold. The thresholds decrease to 2/5: at δ=2/5 each finite sum is 2[1−(2/5)ᵀ]<2, but for every δ>2/5 the infinite sum exceeds 2, so a sufficiently long finite sum does too. At the limiting cutoff, an infinite grim punishment works while every finite T fails.

At δ=1/2,T=2, the values (VC,P₁,P₂) are (8,5,7/2). A cooperative deviation is worth 31/4, below 8. A punishment deviation is worth 3/4, below both 5 and 7/2. By contrast T=1 gives a cooperative deviation worth 17/2, above 8. The reset policy and punishment duration both matter; checking only the on-path payoff would miss this comparison.

7. A fully proved public-lottery cooperation theorem

With a common δ, any normalized repeated-game payoff lies in the convex hull of the finitely many stage payoff vectors: its weights are the expected discounted frequencies (1−δ)ΣδᵗPr(aᵗ=a), which are nonnegative and sum to one. Different player discounts need not generate the same vector of weights, so this joint feasibility argument uses the common-discount assumption.

There is also an individual security restriction in the present public-history game. Define v̲i=minα₋ᵢ∈∏ⱼ≠ᵢΔ(Aⱼ) maxaᵢ∈Aᵢui(ai,α−i). Finite simplices and continuity ensure the minimum exists. Conditional on a public history and public signal, opponents’ current behavioral draws are independent with a known product distribution. A player can best respond at that history and secure at least v̲i then, regardless of the ensuing history; doing so every period secures at least v̲i in normalized value. Therefore a Nash equilibrium payoff cannot be below that level. This is a necessary bound for the specified information/randomization model, not proof that a punishment attaining it is credible for the other players.

Restricted Nash-reversion folk theorem. In a finite stage game let α be a stage Nash equilibrium with payoff r. Each period an exogenous finite-support iid public lottery announces a pure profile a before actions. Its probabilities define a target v=E[u(a)] with vi>ri for every player. Define the largest positive current gain over supported recommendations by

Γi=maxa in lottery support, a′ᵢ∈Aᵢ[ui(a′ᵢ,a−i)−ui(a)] ≥0.

Start in a cooperative state, follow every public recommendation, and remain cooperative only if the announced profile is played. After any departure, play α independently every period forever; this punishment state is absorbing regardless of signals or later actions. This is SPE whenever, for every i,

(1−δ)Γi ≤ δ(vi−ri), equivalently δ ≥ Γi / [Γi+vi−ri].

Proof. After a supported public announcement a in the cooperative state, obedience gives normalized conditional value (1−δ)ui(a)+δvi. A one-shot departure to a′i gives (1−δ)ui(a′i,a−i)+δri. The displayed inequality rules out every such gain, including at recommendations whose current payoff is low. At every punishment history, continuation is unchanged by an action, and α is a stage Nash equilibrium, so no deviation gains there either. Mixed deviations are averages of pure ones. The discounted one-shot principle proves SPE on the tree including the public signals. Before each fresh cooperative draw the normalized value is exactly v, since the draws are iid and play stays cooperative. Finiteness makes Γ finite; strict surplus makes each cutoff strictly below 1. Thus sufficiently patient players sustain this target. This is a full constructive result with an explicit patience bound.

The punishment need not minimize a deviator’s payoff, but it is credible for everyone. Stronger folk theorems replace surplus over a particular Nash payoff by surplus over minmax and add conditions ensuring punishers themselves have incentives; versions also vary with feasible-set dimension and monitoring. We have not proved that broader theorem or a private-monitoring extension. The inspected Manea pages 64–67 distinguish the Nash-reversion construction from those broader claims. Feasibility, individual security, credible punishment, observable deviation, public randomization, strict surplus and patience play different roles.

Worked case 5: a public lottery rewards the current loser later

Row / columnAB
A(2,2)(0,5)
B(5,0)(1,1)

B strictly dominates A: it gains 3 against A and 1 against B. The unique stage Nash and the individual security payoffs are both (1,1). A fair public draw recommends AB or BA with probability 1/2 each, producing target (5/2,5/2). A player told to use B against A already receives 5; changing to A would lower its current payoff to 2. The player told to use A against B receives 0 and can gain 1 by switching to B. Thus Γ₁=Γ₂=1, and the exact recommendation constraints require δ≥2/5. The current loser complies because obeying preserves a future lottery worth more than Nash reversion. An average-payoff comparison before the signal would not alone verify this conditional incentive.

Now announce AB with probability λ=1/3 and BA with 2/3. The target becomes (10/3,5/3). Both players still face a supported losing recommendation and a maximum gain of 1. Their respective discount thresholds are (3/10,3/5); a common δ must be at least 3/5. Changing only the lottery frequency changes the continuation promises and therefore the incentive constraint.

For 0<λ<1, the general target is (5(1−λ),5λ). Strict surplus over (1,1) requires λ∈(1/5,4/5), and the two thresholds are 1/[5(1−λ)] and 1/(5λ). At either endpoint one player has zero surplus but a supported current temptation of 1, so this Nash-reversion construction fails for every δ<1. That failure does not establish impossibility for every conceivable repeated-game strategy at a weak-security boundary. Outside the closed interval, one target component is below its security payoff, which does give a necessary-condition obstruction in this model.

8. Private commitment can alter a short relationship

Worked case 6: two entrants, one incumbent and an updated prior

There are two periods, a single long-run incumbent and two distinct short-run entrants, each caring only about its own period. Nature chooses the incumbent’s private type once: R is strategic, C is committed. Type C has only the action Fight after entry; this is a primitive action restriction, not a claim that a rational type with an available better action voluntarily chooses a dominated move. The incumbent knows its type. Both entrants observe all earlier public actions and share the prior. In each period the current entrant chooses Out or Enter, and after Enter the incumbent responds Fight or Accommodate. Stage payoffs, listed incumbent then current entrant, are Out (4,0), Fight (−1,−2), Accommodate (1,2). The incumbent discounts period 2 by d=4/5. Here values are the unnormalized two-period sum.

In period 2, R accommodates after every history because 1>−1 and no future remains; C fights by restriction. If the entrant’s posterior probability of C is p, entry pays 2(1−p)−2p=2−4p, versus zero outside. It enters for p<1/2, stays out for p>1/2, and may mix at p=1/2.

Start with prior π=1/3. Consider R fighting with probability q=1/2 after first-period entry. Bayes’ rule then gives posterior C after Fight equal to π/[π+(1−π)q]=1/2. After Accommodate it is zero, since C cannot take that action. After first-period Out it stays π: the entrant did not know the type, so its decision has the same probability under either type. Prescribe period-2 entry with probability e=1/6 after Fight, and entry with probability one after Accommodate or Out.

Verify R’s first response at the information set that would follow entry. Fighting yields −1+d[4(1−e)+e], since in period 2 R gets 4 if entry is deterred and 1 if it accommodates entry. Accommodating now reveals R and yields 1+d. At e=1/6 both equal (9/5,9/5), making the proposed q admissible. The second entrant is indifferent after Fight because its posterior is 1/2; after Accommodate or Out it strictly enters. The first entrant faces Fight probability π+(1−π)q=2/3, so its hypothetical entry payoff is -2/3; it strictly chooses Out. On the equilibrium path, R receives 4+d=24/5 and C receives 4−d=16/5. These incumbent-type values are conditional, not payoffs guaranteed to every participant.

The off-path belief following first-period Fight is consistent, not assigned arbitrarily. For ε∈(0,1/2), let the first entrant enter with ε; keep R’s first fight probability q=1/2; make R fight with ε in period 2 at each public history; let the second entrant enter with 1−ε after Out/Accommodate and with 1/6 after Fight. C still has its singleton Fight action. This is completely mixed relative to every available action set. The first entry tremble is type independent. Consequently Bayes beliefs after Fight, Accommodate and Out are exactly (1/2,0,1/3) for every ε. All these profiles converge to the assessment just verified. Singleton own-type information sets need no extra nontrivial beliefs. The perturbations establish consistency and need not themselves satisfy best responses.

Changed prior. If π=1/5, keep the same posterior 1/2 after Fight by setting q=π/(1−π)=1/4. R’s indifference still requires e=1/6, and the second entrant still enters after Accommodate or Out. Now first-period Fight probability is 2π=2/5, so entry pays 2/5 and the first entrant strictly enters. A consistency sequence uses first entry probability 1−ε instead of ε, with the other trembles as before and q=1/4. Posteriors are exactly (1/2,0,1/5). The on-path incumbent values become (9/5,23/15) for R and C: the latter is −1+(4/5)[4(5/6)−1/6]. Every type, entrant and public history has been specified.

These are two complete sequential assessments, not a classification of all equilibria of every reputation model. The strategic incumbent may fight after hypothetical entry to preserve favorable future beliefs, yet changing the prior here reverses actual first-period entry. No universal benefit of reputation, unique selection theorem or empirical entry-frequency prediction follows. Manea’s reputation discussion on pages 84–87 supplies the commitment-type context; this two-period tree, its payoff units and its two priors are original.

9. Exercises

Use complete contingent strategies, exact fractions and the declared information sets. Label whether a claim concerns one strategy, every equilibrium in a stated class, or a theorem over a whole family of games. The proof questions require the missing steps, not only the theorem names.

  1. Realization equivalence. State perfect recall and prove both directions of finite mixed/behavioral equivalence, including a zero own-prefix probability. For a one-player tree, the first choice is X or Y and, remembering it, the player chooses L or R at a separate information set after each branch. A plan lists (first choice, action after X, action after Y). The mixed plan assigns (X,L,L), (X,R,L), (Y,L,R) probabilities 1/2,1/6,1/3. Find the equivalent behavior and the four terminal probabilities. Explain why unused plan correlations need not agree.
  2. Every threat equilibrium. Derive the complete normal-form Nash set and the unique SPE in case 1. Explain why entry cannot mix with positive probability while the incumbent fights with positive probability. Recompute the SPE correspondence for entry costs k=1,2,3, retaining off-path incumbent behavior.
  3. Bayes at a zero-reach continuation. Verify the stated weak PBE family in case 2. Prove the unique sequential assessment and give an actual completely mixed consistency sequence. Identify the proper subgame and explain the precise implication for the weak-PBE definition used here.
  4. Own probabilities cancel. Prove the cancellation and finite information-set one-shot lemmas, including the positive-reach limiting denominator and zero-effect sets. As a numerical illustration, nature picks H/L with probabilities 1/3,2/3. At h the player cannot observe that state and chooses Go with probability g or Stop. Conditional on Go, a chance trial reaches the player’s later information set k with probabilities 3/4 in H and 1/4 in L; failure ends play. At k the player remembers Go but not the state or a separate signal. Compute its belief for g>0, its consistent limit as g↓0 and the belief after an own deviation to Go from starting h.
  5. Sequential existence. Construct the finite agent-normal game and prove that C06’s perfect-equilibrium sequence supplies a sequential assessment. Show the exact reach-times-conditional-payoff identity, why division is legitimate before the limit, how one common belief subsequence is obtained, and how global continuation optimality follows. Explain why original-player normal-form perfection or agent-form Nash alone cannot replace the argument.
  6. Finite versus infinite cooperation. Prove finite known-horizon unravelling for case 3 and the discounted one-shot deviation principle used for infinite repetition. Derive the grim-trigger cutoff and verify punishment histories. Decide whether grim is SPE when player discounts are 1/3 and 3/4. State the conditions that a changed terminal date or payoff would require you to revisit.
  7. Credible forgiveness. Derive every value and incentive inequality for case 4’s reset automaton. Prove existence and monotonicity of its finite-T threshold and the limit 2/5; distinguish the limit from any finite T. Recompute T=1 and T=2 at δ=1/2, including every punishment state. Do not assume that forgiveness automatically improves enforceability.
  8. A constructive folk theorem. Prove the general public-lottery Nash-reversion result in Section 7, checking incentives after the signal and in the absorbing mixed-Nash punishment. Derive the explicit discount bound and show why strict surplus makes it less than one. Identify exactly what is not supplied about arbitrary minmax punishments or private monitoring.
  9. Unequal lottery promises. Derive the security payoffs, targets and conditional temptation gains in case 5. Compute the thresholds for λ=1/2 and λ=1/3. For a common δ=1/2, find the complete interval of λ∈(0,1) for which this particular construction is SPE. Explain separately what happens at λ=1/5, outside the security interval, and when public recommendations are replaced by private signals without a new monitoring specification.
  10. Reputation after a prior change. Give every strategy and posterior in case 6 for π=1/3 and π=1/5. Derive q and e from Bayes and rational-type indifference, verify all entrant decisions and incumbent responses, construct consistent trembles and recompute both type-specific on-path values. Explain why allowing the commitment type to accommodate with the same payoffs would change the game.
  11. Forgotten exits. A driver chooses Exit or Continue at the first of two exits. Exiting immediately pays 0. Continuing reaches the second exit, where Exit pays 5 and Continue pays 1. The two decision nodes are one information set: the driver does not remember whether it has already passed an exit. With a fresh behavioral probability p of Exit at each visit, derive the expected payoff and its global optimum. Compare every mixed distribution over the two pure plans, always Exit or always Continue. Which hypothesis of the realization proof fails, and where?
  12. Research and institutional critique, 16 points. Audit this memo: “The average cooperative payoff exceeds Nash, so any public or private recommendation is enforceable when players are patient. Bayes imposes no restriction after a zero-probability action. A small commitment probability guarantees profitable deterrence, and observed non-entry identifies that probability. The folk theorem proves our punishment policy.” Produce a conditional replacement recommendation with a calculation or counterexample for each central claim, an explicit information/strategy contract, and a feasible evidence plan. Do not assert an empirical conclusion from the synthetic games.
Complete solutions and scoring guidance

  1. Perfect recall makes the ordered list of own past information sets and actions identical at all nodes of any current information set. It prevents revisiting an information set along a path. Given behavior, draw one action independently at every own set to obtain plan probability ∏b(a|h). Along a terminal path each set is used at most once, so summing out unused coordinates gives precisely the behavioral path probability. Given a mixed plan distribution, condition it at h on plans agreeing with the common remembered own prefix R(h); the probability of action a is m({s∈R(h):s(h)=a})/m(R(h)). Along a terminal path these prefix probabilities telescope. If a prefix has probability zero, the first action entering such a prefix has behavioral probability zero, and arbitrary behavior afterward cannot change any terminal mass. Multiplying by the unchanged chance and opponent factors proves realization equivalence against every opponent profile.

    In the stated mixture, X has probability 1/2+1/6=2/3 and Y has 1/3. Conditional on X, L has probability (1/2)/(2/3)=3/4 and R has 1/4. Conditional on Y, R is certain. Thus the terminal probabilities in order XL,XR,YL,YR are (1/2,1/6,0,1/3). Forming independent products over behavioral choices can give a different distribution over the eight complete plans, but every used path has the same probability. Actions specified at an unreached branch do not by themselves identify those unused correlations.

  2. Let x=Pr(In), f=Pr(Fight). The entrant’s In payoff is 4−5f, versus 2 outside. The incumbent’s ex ante gain from A instead of F is x[1−(−2)]=3x. If x>0 it must accommodate, so f=0 and the entrant strictly chooses In: (x,f)=(1,0). If x=0, the incumbent is indifferent across all contingent responses and Out is a best reply exactly when 4−5f≤2, or f∈[2/5,1]. These cases exhaust x∈[0,1]. A positive entry probability with positive fight probability violates the incumbent’s best-response condition even at the entrant’s indifference value f=2/5.

    The proper subgame after In requires A because 1>−2. The entrant then chooses In because 4>2, proving the unique SPE. With cost k, the incumbent’s comparison is unchanged and the entrant compares 4−k with 2. At k=1 it enters; at k=2 it may mix arbitrarily; at k=3 it stays out. In all three cases its complete SPE response specifies A if entry occurs. Different normal-form threats producing the same Out outcome are not additional subgame-perfect responses.

  3. Given belief θ, player 2 prefers A weakly exactly when 3θ≥2(1−θ), namely θ≥2/5. With A prescribed, player 1 prefers Stop’s 1 to Continue’s 0. Stop makes player 2’s information set unreached, so Bayes at positive-reach sets alone adds no condition there. This verifies the stated weak PBE family; it does not purport to enumerate every weak PBE mixture at equality.

    For any positive Continue probability c, the two node probabilities are c/3 and 2c/3. Their conditional ratio is always 1/3. Every common completely mixed sequence therefore has limiting belief 1/3. Player 2 then receives 1 from A and 4/3 from B, so B is uniquely optimal; player 1 receives 3 by continuing instead of 1 by stopping. The assessment is uniquely Continue,B,θ=1/3. Choose both prescribed actions with probability 1−ε and alternatives with ε, keeping nature fixed, to give an explicit consistent sequence. After Continue, the singleton chance node and its descendants form a proper subgame that includes player 2’s whole information set. Its equilibrium also forces B. Thus our weak PBE Stop,A is not SPE. Other definitions of PBE need their own conditions before any hierarchy is stated.

  4. Fix a consistent (b,μ), a starting own information set h, and a changed continuation β. If a later own set k follows h at any node, perfect recall puts an h predecessor and the same intervening own information/action sequence before every node of k. Along each completely mixed approximation bⁿ, those own action probabilities factor identically across all nodes of k and cancel in Bayes’ rule. Starting at h with μⁿh and replacing own continuation by β multiplies each k-node weight by a common factor: the ratio of its intervening β own-action product to its bⁿ product, divided by the common probability of h. If the limiting changed continuation reaches k positively, the required β probabilities are positive. Conditioning gives μⁿk for every n. Finite path probabilities converge; a strictly positive limiting conditional-reach denominator lets the ratio converge to the actual changed-plan conditional distribution. Hence it equals μk. No division by zero equilibrium reach was used.

    For a purported profitable continuation, take a last own information set at which it differs from b under the acyclic successor order. Future own behavior there is already b. If it is reached, its actual belief is μ at that set, so the local one-shot inequality permits replacing its current action by b without lowering payoff from h. If it is not reached, the replacement has zero effect. Repeat finitely many times to replace the whole deviation, contradicting profitability. Current mixed actions are convex combinations of pure actions, and the realization argument covers mixed contingent plans. This proves the one-shot lemma’s sufficiency; necessity is immediate from the allowed deviation class.

    Numerically, the node masses at k are (1/3)g(3/4)=g/4 and (2/3)g(1/4)=g/6. Their sum is 5g/12, giving H probability 3/5 for every g>0. The same ratio is the consistent limit when Go tends to probability zero. If the player instead goes for certain from starting h with its prior belief, the masses are 1/4 and 1/6, again giving 3/5. The player can change whether k is reached; it cannot learn the hidden state by changing its own state-independent action probability.

  5. Create one finite agent for every original player-information-set pair h, with action set A(h) and the original owner’s terminal utility. A mixed agent profile is independent behavior at the tree’s information sets. C06 supplies a perfect agent profile b and fully mixed tⁿ→b such that bh is best against tⁿ−h for every agent. The latter opponents include other agents belonging to the same original player. Positive chance probabilities and completely mixed actions give Ptⁿ(h)>0. Perfect recall prevents a current h action from changing its own prior reach. For any local alternative qh, the ex ante payoff difference is exactly

    Ptⁿ(h)[Ui(bh,tⁿ−h|h,μⁿh)−Ui(qh,tⁿ−h|h,μⁿh)] ≥0.

    Divide by the positive factor at each finite n. The finite collection of belief simplices is compact, so one subsequence converges simultaneously at all information sets to μ. Conditional payoff is a finite continuous sum, giving all local inequalities in the limit. The sequence ensures consistency by definition, and Exercise 4 upgrades local to full continuation optimality. This proves sequential existence on the stated finite perfect-recall, structurally pruned tree.

    Original-player mixed plans can correlate mistakes at different information sets, so perfection there is a different refinement and does not supply these independent agent trembles. Agent-form Nash by itself also permits every action to be an ex ante best reply at an unreached information set, even a conditionally inferior one. The positive-reach perturbation and division address exactly that problem; omitting them would leave the proof incomplete.

  6. In the stage game, D pays 2 more than C against either action. At the last date of a finite commonly known horizon, DD is therefore uniquely required after every history. Its payoff is independent of earlier play. Inducting backward, continuation play at every later date is already fixed at DD, so each earlier stage again requires DD. Positive discounting retains the continuation players’ utility comparisons. The claim assumes a fixed complete-information repetition with additive payoffs and no changed terminal incentives.

    For the infinite one-shot principle, a profitable deviation of normalized gain ε can be truncated after K stages at cost at most 2Mδᴷ. Choose K with that bound below ε/2. The truncated deviation remains profitable, yet eliminating its last deviations one finite stage at a time cannot lower value if every one-shot inequality holds. This ends at the prescribed strategy and contradicts profitability. Finite public signals simply enlarge the finite histories at each truncated stage; their realized values must be included when checking local incentives.

    At a grim cooperative history, 4/(1−δ)≥6+δ/(1−δ) is equivalent to 4≥6−5δ and hence δ≥2/5. In the absorbing punishment state, D earns 1 instead of −1 with no continuation effect, so it is strictly optimal. Thus the proposed grim profile is SPE exactly when each player’s discount meets the cutoff. With discounts 1/3 and 3/4, the first player fails it, so the profile is not SPE despite the second player’s patience. Unknown/random stopping, different terminal payoffs, unobserved actions or other continuation equilibria require their respective belief, payoff and observability arguments to be rebuilt.

  7. The compliant cooperative value is VC=4/(1−δ). After k remaining DD periods, Pk=Σj=0k−1δʲ+δᵏVC, with P₀=VC. At C, the deviation gains 2 immediately and replaces next period’s VC by PT. Hence it is deterred exactly when 2≤δ(VC−PT)=3Σt=1Tδᵗ. During Pk, a deviation loses 2 currently and resets to PT instead of Pk−1. Since Pk−1≥PT, obedience gains at least 2 there. This checks every automaton state and every unilateral action; simultaneous departures have their specified reset continuation too.

    The cooperation polynomial is strictly increasing between zero and one, with endpoint values 0 and 3T, so there is exactly one crossing of 2. T=1 yields 2/3; T=2 solves 3δ²+3δ−2=0 and gives (√33−3)/6. Adding a term strictly lowers the root. At δ=2/5 the finite value is 2[1−(2/5)ᵀ], below 2, so all finite roots exceed 2/5. For any larger δ the infinite sum exceeds 2; a finite partial sum eventually does too, proving convergence of roots to 2/5. The finite-T cutoff never equals its infinite limit.

    At δ=1/2, VC=8, P₁=1+8/2=5 and P₂=1+5/2=7/2. With T=2, a cooperative deviation earns 6+(7/2)/2=31/4<8. In either punishment state its deviation payoff is −1+(7/2)/2=3/4, below P₁=5 and P₂=7/2. With T=1, the cooperative deviation instead earns 6+5/2=17/2>8. A shorter forgiving punishment sacrifices deterrence in this example; its moral label is not an incentive calculation.

  8. Let the public finite iid draw recommend a pure profile a with expected payoff v, and choose a stage Nash α with payoff r. Before any departure, follow the recommendation; after any departure, enter an absorbing state playing α every period regardless of signals and further actions. At a cooperative realized-signal history, obeying gives (1−δ)ui(a)+δvi; departing to a′i gives (1−δ)ui(a′i,a−i)+δri. Thus every pure deviation is deterred if (1−δ)Γi≤δ(vi−ri). Rearranging gives the stated Γi/[Γi+vi−ri] bound. Strict surplus and finite Γ make it less than one, including the Γ=0 case with bound zero.

    At punishment histories, α is a stage Nash best reply and the future punishment value is action independent. No current departure helps there. The discounted one-shot principle therefore proves SPE at all histories, including announcements that temporarily disadvantage a player. Since each future cooperative draw has the same distribution, its before-draw value is v. This construction needs observable action departures from public pure recommendations, credible Nash reversion, iid public randomization, bounded utility and sufficient patience. Arbitrary minmax punishments may not be optimal for the punishers; the proof has supplied no reward scheme to fix that. Private recommendations or noisy/private monitoring change what is known and detected, so the same inequalities and state transitions cannot be presumed valid.

  9. B strictly dominates A, gaining 3 against A and 1 against B. Against an opponent who uses A with probability t, B earns 5t+1(1−t)=1+4t, minimized at t=0 with value 1. Thus each player’s security payoff and the unique Nash payoff are 1. A public lottery assigning AB probability λ gives row player 5(1−λ) and column player 5λ. At a losing A recommendation, changing to B gains 1; at a winning B recommendation, changing to A loses 3. With both signals supported, Γ₁=Γ₂=1.

    The thresholds are δ≥1/[5(1−λ)] and δ≥1/(5λ). For λ=1/2 they are both 2/5 and the target is (5/2,5/2). For λ=1/3 they are 3/10 and 3/5 and the target is (10/3,5/3). Setting δ=1/2 gives λ≤3/5 and λ≥2/5, so the complete supported interval for this construction is [2/5,3/5], including both equality endpoints. This is sharper than merely requiring positive surplus.

    At λ=1/5 the column target is 1, equal to its punishment payoff; after a losing recommendation its current temptation is still 1, so no δ<1 deters it under this construction. At λ outside [1/5,4/5] one player is promised less than its security payoff, contradicting the necessary Nash bound in the specified public-history model. At a weak-security endpoint, failure of this one construction is not a general impossibility theorem. With private signals, a player may not know the other recommendation and others may not detect a departure; conditional beliefs, signal laws and punishments must be specified and reverified before any enforceability claim.

  10. R accommodates in period 2 at every public history, while C has only Fight. Entry at a posterior p pays 2−4p, giving cutoff 1/2. If R fights with q in period 1, the posterior after Fight is π/[π+(1−π)q]. Setting it to 1/2 requires q=π/(1−π). The posterior after Accommodate is zero and after Out is π, since the first entrant’s action is independent of the hidden type. At a mixed second-entry probability e after Fight, R’s first Fight value is −1+(4/5)(4−3e); its Accommodate value is 1+4/5=9/5. Equality gives e=1/6. These conditions deliver q=1/2 at π=1/3 and q=1/4 at π=1/5, both strictly interior.

    For either prior, the second entrant can mix at 1/6 after Fight because p=1/2, and strictly enters after Accommodate or Out because the relevant p is 0 or π<1/2. The first entrant’s Fight probability is π+(1−π)q=2π, making its expected entry payoff 2−8π. This equals −2/3 at π=1/3, so Out is strict, and 2/5 at π=1/5, so Enter is strict. R’s first response is indifferent, its last response strictly accommodates, and C has no discretionary response. This checks all strategic information sets.

    For consistency choose ε↓0; perturb the first entrant’s entry probability to ε for the baseline or 1−ε for the changed prior, retain the appropriate interior q, let R fight with ε in period 2 at each history, retain second-entry probability 1/6 after Fight and use 1−ε after Out/Accommodate. C’s singleton action remains Fight. Bayes gives the exact posteriors (1/2,0,π) throughout the sequence because the entry tremble is type independent and C cannot accommodate. The limiting assessments are therefore sequential equilibria; the trembled profiles themselves need not be equilibria.

    At baseline, first-period Out gives R value 4+(4/5)·1=24/5 and C value 4+(4/5)(−1)=16/5, since period-2 entry occurs after Out. At π=1/5 the first entrant enters. R’s mixed response averages two values 9/5, so it receives 9/5. C fights and then faces second entry with probability 1/6, giving −1+(4/5)[(5/6)4+(1/6)(−1)]=23/15. Allowing C to accommodate with these same utilities would remove its primitive commitment: in the final period it would strictly prefer accommodation. The belief and incentive system would have to be solved for that different game, not inherited from this one.

  11. First Exit occurs with probability p and pays 0. Reaching the second exit and exiting has probability (1−p)p and pays 5; continuing twice has probability (1−p)² and pays 1. The expected value is 5p(1−p)+(1−p)²=1+3p−4p². Completing the square gives 25/16−4(p−3/8)². Hence the unique global maximum on [0,1] has (3/8,25/16) for (p,value).

    A pure plan for the single information set must specify the same action whenever it is visited. Always Exit ends immediately with 0; always Continue passes both exits and gives 1. Any ex ante mixture of those two plans averages their payoffs and gives at most 1. It cannot reproduce the behavioral optimum 25/16. The two nodes in one information set have different remembered own histories: at the second the player has already continued at that very set. Perfect recall and the no-revisit consequence both fail. In the behavioral-to-plan argument, one fixed sampled action cannot substitute for fresh independent draws at two visits to the same set; in the reverse direction there is no single common remembered prefix to condition upon.

  12. Illustrative corrected recommendation. Specify the action sets, payoff units, observability of past actions and current recommendations, discounting, state transitions after every departure, and any true commitment restrictions. Then check each player’s conditional deviation gain against its own continuation loss at every cooperative and punishment history. Case 5’s fair lottery needs δ≥2/5, but changing its frequency to λ=1/3 raises one player’s bound to 3/5. At δ=1/2 it therefore fails despite both average payoffs exceeding Nash. A private recommendation would require a different information and detection model; it cannot inherit the public-signal calculation.

    The claim about beliefs is false in case 2: every positive Continue tremble gives H probability 1/3, even when Continue has limiting probability zero. Case 6 likewise pins down (1/2,0,π) through one completely mixed sequence. Its prior change reverses first-period entry, so a “small” commitment probability has no universal deterrence implication. The commitment type’s action restriction, available choices, entrant horizons and posterior-dependent continuation all matter. Observed non-entry alone could also reflect costs, payoffs, information or another equilibrium selection; it does not identify π.

    Finally, the proved restricted folk result verifies a public-lottery/Nash-reversion strategy under explicit surplus and patience conditions. It supplies neither credibility of an arbitrary punishment policy nor a theorem for every minmax or private-monitoring environment. A feasible evidence plan would measure or bound payoffs and timing, document what each party observes and which responses it can implement, and test alternative information/commitment models using observations that distinguish their predicted conditional actions. Report sensitivity and possible nonidentification; synthetic payoff arithmetic is not empirical validation. Other defensible recommendations earn credit if they state their additional assumptions and consequences.

    Scoring, 16 points. Use four domains worth 4 points each: conditional/current versus continuation incentives; consistent beliefs and information; commitment, prior sensitivity and identification; proved theorem scope and implementable evidence. In each domain award 1 point for the correct distinction, 1 for a relevant exact calculation or counterexample, 1 for stating the additional condition needed by the recommendation, and 1 for a coherent consequence or evidence test. A bare theorem name or ethical preference earns no substitute credit for a missing incentive or information argument.

10. Teach-back and delayed retention

Teach-back. Explain to a colleague why “punishment deters deviation” is incomplete. A complete answer identifies the deviator’s immediate gain, its discounted continuation loss, the punishers’ own incentives, and the information needed to detect a departure. Compare grim, the two-period reset punishment and the public lottery. A high average value before a recommendation does not establish obedience after it.

Retention prompts. (i) Why does agent-form perfection involve several agents with the same utility? (ii) Why can a zero-probability continuation still have a uniquely consistent belief? (iii) At δ=2/5, does some finite reset punishment sustain case 3’s cooperation? (iv) Why is a forced commitment type not a rational player choosing a dominated action?

Answers. (i) Each information set chooses and trembles separately while retaining its original owner’s payoff; positive perturbed reach yields conditional local incentives, then perfect recall closes the continuation proof. (ii) The same completely mixed sequence must generate all beliefs; common reach factors can cancel as in case 2, leaving nature’s odds fixed. (iii) No: every finite sum equals 2[1−(2/5)ᵀ]<2, while grim’s infinite loss reaches the required 2. (iv) The commitment type has a singleton feasible action. Giving it accommodation would change the game and invalidate the inherited posterior and response calculations.

Reproduction. Start from the tree, payoff tables and type restrictions. Compute conditional node masses before normalizing beliefs; derive strategy values from their transition equations; enumerate every action at each finite automaton state; and verify reputation decisions after Out, Fight and Accommodate separately. Editorial standard-library checks reconstruct the finite calculations, policy comparisons and domains. These numerical witnesses accompany the general proofs and do not replace them or establish empirical predictions.

11. Scope and the next information problem

The author added actual scoped inspection of the retained Manea and Yildiz primary PDFs, reusing their existing source identities and exact URLs. Manea’s relevant extensive-game, one-shot, assessment, agent-form, Nash-reversion and reputation passages were read, with five selected proof-page images inspected; Yildiz’s remembered-history, assessment and agent-form passages were cross-checked, with two selected equation-page images. Neither whole document is claimed read. Manea’s one-shot adaptation gap is filled here by a complete finite information-set argument. The source’s broad minmax, generic converse, proper-equilibrium and long-run reputation results are not claimed as proved by this chapter. All six numerical cases and the additional exercises are original library constructions.

Next. Information economics and screening makes private information itself the object of contract design. The participation and incentive constraints of a menu, or the beliefs following a signal, depend on the same discipline used here: actual action rights, complete contingent responses and a specified information structure.
